claim: Color vision in birds is mediated by four types of cone photoreceptors whose maximal sensitivities (λmax) are evenly spaced across the light spectrum.
source: Color vision in birds is mediated by four types of cone photoreceptors whose maximal sensitivities (λmax) are evenly spaced across the light spectrum.
evidence: This is a general statement about avian color vision that draws from established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: In the course of avian evolution, the λmax of the most shortwave-sensitive cone, SWS1, has switched between violet (λmax > 400 nm) and ultraviolet (λmax < 380 nm) multiple times.
source: In the course of avian evolution, the λmax of the most shortwave-sensitive cone, SWS1, has switched between violet (λmax > 400 nm) and ultraviolet (λmax < 380 nm) multiple times.
evidence: This statement references established findings in the literature about evolutionary transitions in avian vision.

claim: The shift of the SWS1 opsin is accompanied by a corresponding short-wavelength shift in the spectrally adjacent SWS2 cone.
source: This shift of the SWS1 opsin is accompanied by a corresponding short-wavelength shift in the spectrally adjacent SWS2 cone.
evidence: This is a key finding of the study supported by data presented in the manuscript.

claim: SWS2 cone spectral tuning is mediated by modulating the ratio of two apocarotenoids, galloxanthin and 11',12'-dihydrogalloxanthin, which act as intracellular spectral filters in this cell type.
source: Here, we show that SWS2 cone spectral tuning is mediated by modulating the ratio of two apocarotenoids, galloxanthin and 11',12'-dihydrogalloxanthin, which act as intracellular spectral filters in this cell type.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by biochemical and spectroscopic data.

claim: Correlated evolution of spectral tuning is necessary to achieve even sampling of the light spectrum and thereby maintain near-optimal color discrimination.
source: we use color vision modeling to demonstrate how correlated evolution of spectral tuning is necessary to achieve even sampling of the light spectrum and thereby maintain near-optimal color discrimination.
evidence: This claim is supported by computational modeling results presented in the manuscript.

claim: Visual pigments consist of a retinoid chromophore bound to an opsin protein.
source: Color vision systems are based on visual pigments consisting of a retinoid chromophore bound to an opsin protein (Yokoyama, 2000).
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field, supported by a citation.

claim: The peak spectral sensitivity of the visual pigment is determined by the amino acid composition of the opsin and the structure of the chromophore.
source: The peak spectral sensitivity of the visual pigment is determined by the amino acid composition of the opsin and the structure of the chromophore (Yokoyama, 2000; Wang et al., 2014; Bridges, 1972).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: Color vision is achieved by comparing the stimulation of receptors that are maximally sensitive to different wavelengths of light.
source: Color vision is achieved by comparing the stimulation of receptors that are maximally sensitive to different wavelengths of light (Goldsmith, 1990), but overlap of the receptors' sensitivity spectra limits color discrimination (Govardovskii et al., 2000; Dyer, 1999; Vorobyev and Osorio, 1998; Vorobyev, 2003).
evidence: This is established knowledge in color vision theory, supported by citations.

claim: Overlap of the receptors' sensitivity spectra limits color discrimination.
source: Color vision is achieved by comparing the stimulation of receptors that are maximally sensitive to different wavelengths of light (Goldsmith, 1990), but overlap of the receptors' sensitivity spectra limits color discrimination (Govardovskii et al., 2000; Dyer, 1999; Vorobyev and Osorio, 1998; Vorobyev, 2003).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: Birds have overcome the limitation of spectral overlap by narrowing the spectral bandwidth of some of their photoreceptors through the use of a specialized optical organelle, the pigmented cone oil droplet.
source: Birds have overcome this limitation by narrowing the spectral bandwidth of some of their photoreceptors through the use of a specialized optical organelle, the pigmented cone oil droplet (Figure 1a–b).
evidence: This is established knowledge about avian vision, with reference to figures showing oil droplets.

claim: Cone oil droplets are located in the path of light through the receptor and act as long-pass cutoff filters matched to the visual pigment sensitivity of each cone subtype.
source: These oil droplets are located in the path of light through the receptor and act as long-pass cutoff filters matched to the visual pigment sensitivity of each cone subtype.
evidence: This describes the functional role of oil droplets based on established knowledge.

claim: Light filtering by the droplet narrows the spectral bandwidth of receptor sensitivity, thereby reducing sensitivity overlap between spectrally adjacent cone types.
source: Light filtering by the droplet narrows the spectral bandwidth of receptor sensitivity, thereby reducing sensitivity overlap between spectrally adjacent cone types (Figure 1c–d).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in the referenced figures.

claim: Oil droplet filtering enhances color discrimination and color constancy.
source: Theoretical considerations suggest that this adaptation enhances color discrimination and color constancy (Vorobyev, 2003; Vorobyev et al., 1998).
evidence: This is based on theoretical modeling supported by citations.

claim: All birds can be classified into two groups: violet-sensitive species (VS), whose most short-wavelength sensitive cone (SWS1) is maximally sensitive to violet light (λmax > 400 nm), and ultraviolet-sensitive species (UVS), whose SWS1 cone is maximally sensitive to ultraviolet light (λmax < 380 nm).
source: All birds can be classified into two groups: violet-sensitive species (VS), whose most short-wavelength sensitive cone (SWS1) is maximally sensitive to violet light (λmax > 400 nm), and ultraviolet-sensitive species (UVS), whose SWS1 cone is maximally sensitive to ultraviolet light (λmax < 380 nm) (Cuthill et al., 2000; Ödeen and Håstad, 2003; 2013; Shi et al., 2001).
evidence: This is established knowledge in avian vision research, supported by multiple citations.

claim: The switch between violet and ultraviolet sensitivity has occurred at least 14 times in the course of avian evolution.
source: In the course of avian evolution, the switch between violet and ultraviolet sensitivity has occurred at least 14 times (Ödeen and Håstad, 2013).
evidence: This is a specific finding from the cited literature.

claim: The essence of the VS to UVS switch is a short-wavelength shift in the peak sensitivity of the SWS1 opsin that can be mediated by as little as a single amino acid substitution (e.g. S90C) in the second transmembrane helix.
source: The essence of this switch is a short-wavelength shift in the peak sensitivity of the SWS1 opsin that can be mediated by as little as a single amino acid substitution (e.g. S90C) in the second transmembrane helix (Shi et al., 2001; Altun et al., 2011; Hauser et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge from molecular studies, supported by citations.

claim: The short-wavelength shift of the SWS1 cone expands the spectral sensitivity of the visual system and is predicted to enhance color discrimination.
source: This short-wavelength shift of the SWS1 cone expands the spectral sensitivity of the visual system and is predicted to enhance color discrimination (Vorobyev et al., 1998; Cuthill et al., 2000).
evidence: This is based on theoretical predictions supported by citations.

claim: A shift in the SWS1 cone alone disrupts the even spacing of receptor sensitivities across the visible spectrum and necessitates corresponding shifts in the sensitivity of the other single cone photoreceptors to maintain even spacing.
source: However, a shift in the SWS1 cone alone disrupts the even spacing of receptor sensitivities across the visible spectrum and necessitates corresponding shifts in the sensitivity of the other single cone photoreceptors to maintain even spacing.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the requirements for optimal color vision.

claim: Between VS and UVS species, the sensitivity of the short-wavelength sensitive 2 (SWS2) cone is tuned to maximize its spectral separation from the adjacent SWS1 and medium-wavelength sensitive (MWS) cones.
source: Accordingly, between VS and UVS species, the sensitivity of the short-wavelength sensitive 2 (SWS2) cone is tuned to maximize its spectral separation from the adjacent SWS1 and medium-wavelength sensitive (MWS) cones (Figure 1c–e).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in the referenced figures.

claim: The spectral shift of the SWS2 cone is driven primarily by changes in the filtering of the C-type oil droplet, in contrast to the opsin-mediated shift of the SWS1 cone sensitivity.
source: However, in contrast to the opsin-mediated shift of the SWS1 cone sensitivity, the spectral shift of the SWS2 cone is driven primarily by changes in the filtering of the C-type oil droplet (Hart and Vorobyev, 2005).
evidence: This is established knowledge from the cited literature.

claim: Among bird species, there is a strong positive correlation between the spectral sensitivity of the SWS1 opsin and the spectral cut-off wavelength of oil droplet filtering in the SWS2 cone.
source: Among bird species, there is a strong positive correlation between the spectral sensitivity of the SWS1 opsin and the spectral cut-off wavelength of oil droplet filtering in the SWS2 cone (Figure 1f) (Hart and Vorobyev, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1f and cited literature.

claim: Distinct mechanisms of spectral tuning are coordinated to ensure even sampling of the visible spectrum.
source: This finding suggests that distinct mechanisms of spectral tuning are coordinated to ensure even sampling of the visible spectrum.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the correlation data.

claim: Cone oil droplets are pigmented with carotenoids, a class of terpenoid molecules whose light absorption properties are determined by their degree of π-electron conjugation.
source: It has long been known that cone oil droplets are pigmented with carotenoids, a class of terpenoid molecules whose light absorption properties are determined by their degree of π-electron conjugation (Capranica, 1877; Goldsmith et al., 1984; Chábera et al., 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by historical and recent citations.

claim: Birds cannot synthesize carotenoids de novo and must acquire them through their diet.
source: Birds cannot synthesize carotenoids de novo and must acquire them through their diet (McGraw, 2006).
evidence: This is established knowledge in avian physiology, supported by a citation.

claim: Birds can metabolize diet-derived carotenoids to change their degree of conjugation and thereby shift their absorption spectrum toward longer or shorter wavelengths.
source: However, birds can metabolize these diet-derived carotenoids to change their degree of conjugation and thereby shift their absorption spectrum toward longer or shorter wavelengths (Schiedt, 1998; Bhosale et al., 2007).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The C-type oil droplets within the SWS2 cone of birds is pigmented with apocarotenoids, which are believed to be products of the asymmetrical oxidative cleavage of dietary precursor carotenoids.
source: The C-type oil droplets within the SWS2 cone of birds is pigmented with apocarotenoids, which are believed to be products of the asymmetrical oxidative cleavage of dietary precursor carotenoids (Goldsmith et al., 1984; Toomey et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by previous research including the authors' own work.

claim: Apocarotenoids have relatively short systems of conjugation and specifically absorb short-wavelength light.
source: These molecules have relatively short systems of conjugation and specifically absorb short-wavelength light (Goldsmith et al., 1984; Toomey et al., 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge about apocarotenoid properties, supported by citations.

claim: In the violet-sensitive chicken (Gallus gallus), the C-type droplet contains primarily galloxanthin with a peak absorbance at 402 nm as well as an apocarotenoid of undetermined structure (Apo2) with short-wavelength-shifted peak absorbance at 380 nm.
source: In the violet-sensitive chicken (Gallus gallus), the C-type droplet contains primarily galloxanthin with a peak absorbance at 402 nm as well as an apocarotenoid of undetermined structure (Apo2) with short-wavelength-shifted peak absorbance at 380 nm (Figure 2a) (Toomey et al., 2015).
evidence: This is based on previous research by the authors, with data shown in Figure 2a.

claim: The shift in the spectral tuning of the SWS2 cone between VS and UVS species is mediated by the differential accumulation of galloxanthin and Apo2 (dihydrogalloxanthin) in the C-type cone oil droplet.
source: Here, we hypothesized that the shift in the spectral tuning of the SWS2 cone between VS and UVS species is mediated by the differential accumulation of these two apocarotenoids in the C-type cone oil droplet.
evidence: This is the central hypothesis of the study, tested with biochemical and spectroscopic data.

claim: The absorbance spectrum of Apo2 is short-wavelength shifted by 22 nm relative to galloxanthin, suggesting that Apo2 has fewer conjugated double bonds than galloxanthin.
source: The absorbance spectrum of Apo2 is short-wavelength shifted by 22 nm relative to galloxanthin, suggesting that Apo2 has fewer conjugated double bonds than galloxanthin (Figure 2a).
evidence: This is based on spectroscopic data shown in Figure 2a and inference from conjugation theory.

claim: Apo2 had previously been observed in the retinas of some bird species and was hypothesized to be a truncated (25 carbons) form of galloxanthin (27 carbons) with seven double bonds in conjugation.
source: Apo2 had previously been observed in the retinas of some bird species and was hypothesized to be a truncated (25 carbons) form of galloxanthin (27 carbons) with seven double bonds in conjugation (Goldsmith et al., 1984).
evidence: This is a hypothesis from previous literature.

claim: The absorbance spectrum of a commercial standard of 25-carbon apocarotenoid (fringillixanthin) matched the spectrum of Apo2 almost exactly.
source: To test this hypothesis, we measured the absorbance spectrum of a commercial standard of this 25-carbon apocarotenoid (referred to in the original study as fringillixanthin [Goldsmith et al., 1984]) and found that it matched the spectrum of Apo2 almost exactly (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on experimental spectroscopic measurements shown in the figure supplement.

claim: The molecular weight of Apo2 was two daltons greater than that of galloxanthin.
source: However, when we examined the apocarotenoid profile of the chicken retina by liquid chromatography-mass spectral (LC-MS) analysis, we found that the molecular weight of Apo2 was two daltons greater than that of galloxanthin (Figure 2b; Table 1).
evidence: This is based on LC-MS data shown in Figure 2b and Table 1.

claim: Apo2 has the same number of carbons as galloxanthin but has undergone saturation of one of its double bonds.
source: This finding suggested that Apo2 has the same number of carbons as galloxanthin but has undergone saturation of one of its double bonds.
evidence: This is an inference from the mass spectrometry data.

claim: Saturation of the 11',12' double bond of galloxanthin is predicted to cause a 22.5 nm blue-shift in the wavelength of peak absorbance, a close match to the measured shift of 22 nm observed between Apo2 and galloxanthin.
source: We found that saturation of the 11',12' double bond of galloxanthin is predicted to cause a 22.5 nm blue-shift in the wavelength of peak absorbance, a close match to the measured shift of 22 nm observed between Apo2 and galloxanthin (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is based on theoretical calculations using Woodward-Fieser and Fieser-Kuhn rules, compared to experimental data.

claim: Ozonolysis experiments confirmed that Apo2 is saturated at the 11',12' double bond.
source: The critical product of Apo2 derivatization-ozonolysis had a parent ion and fragmentation pattern identical to that of the standard, confirming the presence of saturation at the 11',12' double bond (Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is based on experimental chemical analysis shown in the figure supplement.

claim: Apo2 is 11',12'-dihydro-10'-Apo-β-carotene-3,10'-diol, which is referred to as dihydrogalloxanthin.
source: These results indicate that Apo2 is 11',12'-dihydro-10'-Apo-β-carotene-3,10'-diol, which we refer to as dihydrogalloxanthin (Figure 2c).
evidence: This is the conclusion from the structural analysis experiments.

claim: Dihydrogalloxanthin was previously observed in the skin of black bass (Micropterus salmoides).
source: This apocarotenoid was previously observed in the skin of black bass (Micropterus salmoides); however, its functional role in that tissue is unknown (Yamashita et al., 1996; Yamashita and Matsuno, 1992).
evidence: This is information from cited literature.

claim: The apocarotenoid ratio (dihydrogalloxanthin:galloxanthin) differed significantly between VS and UVS species.
source: We found that the apocarotenoid ratio (dihydrogalloxanthin:galloxanthin) differed significantly between VS and UVS species (F1,43 = 22.32, p=2.48 x 10−5, Figure 3a).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of HPLC data from multiple species.

claim: UVS species tended to have higher levels of the short wavelength-shifted dihydrogalloxanthin in their retinas (dihydrogalloxanthin:galloxanthin ratio 0.81 ± 0.09) compared to VS species (0.52 ± 0.27).
source: UVS species tended to have higher levels of the short wavelength-shifted dihydrogalloxanthin in their retinas (dihydrogalloxanthin:galloxanthin ratio 0.81 ± 0.09, mean ± SD; n = 21) compared to VS species (0.52 ± 0.27, n = 24, Figure 3a).
evidence: This is based on quantitative HPLC data from multiple species.

claim: The apocarotenoid ratio was subject to strong phylogenetic inertia (Blomberg's K = 1.58, Pagel's λ = 0.93).
source: However, this ratio was subject to strong phylogenetic inertia (Blomberg's K = 1.58, Pagel's λ = 0.93, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic statistical analysis.

claim: SWS1 opsin tuning remained a significant predictor of dihydrogalloxanthin:galloxanthin ratio when accounting for phylogeny (phylogenetic generalized linear model: p=0.012).
source: We therefore repeated the analysis to include phylogeny as part of the model and found that SWS1 opsin tuning remained a significant predictor of dihydrogalloxanthin:galloxanthin ratio (phylogenetic generalized linear model: p=0.012).
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic statistical modeling.

claim: The evolution of the UVS opsin is associated with a relative increase in the concentrations of dihydrogalloxanthin compared to galloxanthin in the retina.
source: Overall, these findings suggest that the evolution of the UVS opsin is associated with a relative increase in the concentrations of dihydrogalloxanthin compared to galloxanthin in the retina.
evidence: This is an inference from the phylogenetic and compositional analyses.

claim: The C-type droplets of UVS species contain primarily dihydrogalloxanthin, while the droplets of the VS species contain primarily galloxanthin.
source: Consistent with our hypothesis, this analysis indicated that the C-type droplets of UVS species contain primarily dihydrogalloxanthin, while the droplets of the VS species contain primarily galloxanthin (Figure 3d–g).
evidence: This is based on microspectrophotometry and spectral curve fitting analysis.

claim: Birds modulate the relative concentrations of galloxanthin and dihydrogalloxanthin in the C-type droplet to shift the spectral filtering of the SWS2 cone, thereby complementing the spectral tuning of the SWS1 cone.
source: Thus, birds appear to modulate the relative concentrations of galloxanthin and dihydrogalloxanthin in the C-type droplet to shift the spectral filtering of the SWS2 cone, thereby complementing the spectral tuning of the SWS1 cone.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the compositional and spectroscopic data.

claim: Radioactive tracer studies indicate that zeaxanthin is the major dietary precursor for the production of galloxanthin in the avian retina.
source: Radioactive tracer studies indicate that zeaxanthin is the major dietary precursor for the production of galloxanthin in the avian retina (Schiedt, 1998; Bhosale et al., 2007), but the enzyme(s) mediating this transformation are currently unknown.
evidence: This is established knowledge from cited literature.

claim: The production of dihydrogalloxanthin involves a three-step metabolic pathway in which zeaxanthin is first cleaved at the 9',10' double bond to generate 3-Hydroxy-10'-apo-β-caroten-10'-al; then the aldehyde group is reduced to produce galloxanthin; and finally the 11',12' double bond of galloxanthin is saturated to produce dihydrogalloxanthin.
source: We hypothesized that the production of dihydrogalloxanthin involves a three-step metabolic pathway in which zeaxanthin is first cleaved at the 9',10' double bond to generate 3-Hydroxy-10'-apo-β-caroten-10'-al; then the aldehyde group is reduced to produce galloxanthin; and finally the 11',12' double bond of galloxanthin is saturated to produce dihydrogalloxanthin (Figure 4a).
evidence: This is a hypothesis tested with enzyme assays shown in Figure 4.

claim: A subpopulation of photoreceptors that included the double cones was significantly enriched for β-carotene oxygenase 2 (BCO2), a known carotenoid cleavage enzyme.
source: In this study, it was reported that a subpopulation of photoreceptors that included the double cones was significantly enriched for β-carotene oxygenase 2 (BCO2), a known carotenoid cleavage enzyme (Enright et al., 2015a; Kiefer et al., 2001; Mein et al., 2010).
evidence: This is information from cited transcriptome studies.

claim: Cells expressing BCO2 and supplemented with zeaxanthin yielded a product consistent with 3-Hydroxy-10'-apo-β-caroten-10'-al, with a characteristic single absorbance peak at 449 nm.
source: Consistent with our hypothesis, cells expressing BCO2 yielded a product consistent with , with a characteristic single absorbance peak at 449 nm (Figure 4d–e).
evidence: This is based on cell culture enzyme assays with HPLC analysis.

claim: Retinol dehydrogenase 12 (RDH12) is the most highly expressed member of the RDH family in LWS opsin-expressing photoreceptors.
source: Further examination of the expression profiles of the LWS opsin-expressing photoreceptors revealed that retinol dehydrogenase 12 (RDH12) is the most highly expressed member of the RDH family (Enright et al., 2015a).
evidence: This is based on transcriptome data from cited literature.

claim: RDH12 is known to act upon a variety of retinal isomers.
source: RDH12 is known to act upon a variety of retinal isomers (Belyaeva et al., 2005).
evidence: This is established knowledge from cited literature.

claim: Co-expression of BCO2 and RDH12 in cells supplemented with zeaxanthin yielded galloxanthin.
source: Consistent with our hypothesis, the co-expression of BCO2 and RDH12 yielded galloxanthin (Figure 4f–g).
evidence: This is based on cell culture enzyme assays with HPLC analysis.

claim: Co-expression of BCO2, RDH12, and RETSAT in cells supplemented with zeaxanthin yielded dihydrogalloxanthin.
source: To test this hypothesis, we cloned RETSAT from the UVS zebra finch and co-expressed it along with BCO2 and RDH12 in HEK293 cells. Supplementation of these cells with zeaxanthin yielded dihydrogalloxanthin, confirming that BCO2, RDH12, and RETSAT are sufficient to produce dihydrogalloxanthin when acting in combination (Figure 4h–i).
evidence: This is based on cell culture enzyme assays with HPLC analysis.

claim: BCO2, RDH12, and RETSAT are sufficient to produce dihydrogalloxanthin when acting in combination.
source: Supplementation of these cells with zeaxanthin yielded dihydrogalloxanthin, confirming that BCO2, RDH12, and RETSAT are sufficient to produce dihydrogalloxanthin when acting in combination (Figure 4h–i).
evidence: This is based on experimental enzyme assays.

claim: Transcripts for BCO2, RDH12, and RETSAT are expressed in the photoreceptor layer of the chicken retina at the time of hatching.
source: We found that transcripts for all three enzymes are expressed in the photoreceptor layer of the retina at the time of hatching (Figure 5a).
evidence: This is based on in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 5a.

claim: Apocarotenoids were first detected in the chicken retina at E18, with levels increasing significantly through the course of development.
source: We first detected apocarotenoids in the retina at E18, with levels increasing significantly through the course of development (galloxanthin: F6,12 = 19.59, p=1.50 x 10−5, dihydrogalloxanthin: F6,12 = 21.00, p=1.03 x 10−5, Figure 5b).
evidence: This is based on HPLC analysis of retinas at different developmental stages.

claim: The transcript levels of BCO2, RDH12, and RETSAT increased significantly through the course of chicken retina development, mirroring the developmental trends in apocarotenoid accumulation.
source: Consistent with their hypothesized role in apocarotenoid metabolism, the transcript levels of BCO2, RDH12, and RETSAT increased significantly through the course of development, mirroring the developmental trends in apocarotenoid accumulation (BCO2: F6,12 = 35.36, p=1.12 x 10−7, RDH12: F6,12 = 19.98, p=4.08 x 10−6, RETSAT: F6,12 = 15.64, p=1.76 x 10−5, Figure 5c).
evidence: This is based on qPCR analysis of retinas at different developmental stages.

claim: BCO2, RDH12, and RETSAT are present in the avian retina and are sufficient to produce galloxanthin and dihydrogalloxanthin from dietary carotenoid precursors in cell culture.
source: Taken together, these results indicate that these enzymes are present in the avian retina and are sufficient to produce galloxanthin and dihydrogalloxanthin from dietary carotenoid precursors in cell culture.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the enzyme expression and activity experiments.

claim: The sensitivity of the SWS2 cone is tuned to facilitate color discrimination and maintain spectral sensitivity across the light spectrum.
source: We hypothesized that the sensitivity of the SWS2 cone is tuned to facilitate color discrimination and maintain spectral sensitivity across the light spectrum.
evidence: This is a hypothesis tested with color vision modeling.

claim: In bright light, the optimal positions of C-type λcut differed significantly between VS and UVS species (independent sample t-test, t = −7.78, p=2.13 x 10−5).
source: In bright light, the optimal positions of C-type λcut differed significantly between VS and UVS species (independent sample t-test, t = −7.78, p=2.13 x 10−5).
evidence: This is based on color vision modeling and statistical analysis.

claim: The optimal positions of the UVS species C-type droplets were short-wavelength shifted (λcut optimal = 425.1 ± 6.5 nm) relative to the optima for the VS species (λcut optimal = 457.4 ± 9.7 nm).
source: The optimal positions of the UVS species were short-wavelength shifted (mean ± SD, λcut optimal = 425.1 ± 6.5 nm, n = 11) relative to the optima for the VS species (λcut optimal = 457.4 ± 9.7 nm, n = 7), a pattern consistent with the actual C-type oil droplet spectral filtering observed within the respective visual systems (Figure 6c–f).
evidence: This is based on color vision modeling results.

claim: In the bright light condition, the modeled optima were highly predictive of actual visual system parameters, differing on average by only 2% in the number of discriminable colors between the optimal and actual spectral filtering.
source: In the bright light condition, the modeled optima were highly predictive of actual visual system parameters, differing on average by only 2% in the number of discriminable colors between the optimal and actual spectral filtering (Figure 6e–f).
evidence: This is based on comparison of modeling predictions to actual measurements.

claim: The number of discriminable colors predicted for the actual visual system parameters of UVS species (8.24 ± 1.77 x 10^6) were significantly greater than the VS species (5.18 ± 1.03 x 10^6) in bright light.
source: Overall, the number of discriminable colors predicted for the actual visual system parameters of UVS species (8.24 ± 1.77 x 106, n = 11) were significantly greater than the VS species (5.18 ± 1.03 x 106, n = 7, independent sample t-test, t = 4.74, p=0.00021, Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on color vision modeling and statistical analysis.

claim: The predicted color discrimination advantage of UVS species is consistent with previous color vision modeling analyses.
source: This predicted color discrimination advantage of UVS species is consistent with a number of previous color vision modeling analyses (Vorobyev et al., 1998; Cuthill et al., 2000).
evidence: This is a comparison to findings in cited literature.

claim: In dim light, the model predicted a significant reduction in the number of discriminable colors compared to the bright-light condition.
source: In dim light, our model predicted a significant reduction in the number of discriminable colors compared to the bright-light condition (Bright: 6.95 ± 2.14 x 106, Dim: 1.29 ± 0.45 x 105, n = 18, paired sample t-test, t = 13.94, p=4.34 x 10−11, Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on color vision modeling under different light conditions.

claim: The actual C-type λcut values underperformed the dim and very dim model optima by 14–25%, which was significantly worse than the fit to the bright-light model.
source: The actual C-type λcut values underperformed the dim and very dim model optima by 14–25%, which was significantly worse than the fit to the bright-light model (mean ± SD proportion of optimal, bright: 0.986 ± 0.016, dim: 0.863 ± 0.057, very dim: 0.745 ± 0.113, n = 18, repeated measures ANOVA, F2,34 = 57.44, p=1.25 x 10−11, Figure 6f).
evidence: This is based on comparison of modeling predictions to actual measurements under different light conditions.

claim: The apocarotenoid-based spectral filtering of the SWS2 cone oil droplet is fine-tuned to facilitate color discrimination in bright-light conditions.
source: These results suggest that the apocarotenoid-based spectral filtering of the SWS2 cone oil droplet is fine-tuned to facilitate color discrimination in bright-light conditions.
evidence: This is an inference from the modeling results showing optimal performance in bright light.

claim: A mismatch of VS species visual systems with UVS-like C-type droplets produced little change in discrimination across the spectrum.
source: When we mismatched the visual systems of VS species with the spectral filtering of UVS-like C-type droplets, our analysis predicted little change in discrimination across the spectrum (Figure 6g).
evidence: This is based on increment threshold spectral sensitivity modeling.

claim: A mismatch of UVS species visual systems with a VS-like C-type droplet produced a spectral 'blind spot' between 400 and 450 nm, where the discrimination is substantially reduced.
source: In contrast, a mismatch of UVS species visual systems with a VS-like C-type droplet produced a spectral 'blind spot' between 400 and 450 nm, where the discrimination is substantially reduced (Figure 6h).
evidence: This is based on increment threshold spectral sensitivity modeling.

claim: The complementary spectral tuning of the SWS2 cone in UVS species, mediated by apocarotenoid-based spectral filtering, is particularly important for the discrimination of spectra that vary in the short-wavelength portions of the light spectrum.
source: These results suggest that the complementary spectral tuning of the SWS2 cone in UVS species, mediated by apocarotenoid-based spectral filtering, is particularly important for the discrimination of spectra that vary in the short-wavelength portions of the light spectrum.
evidence: This is an inference from the increment threshold modeling results.

claim: The majority of bird species rely on vision as their primary sensory modality, and color discrimination plays an important role in essential behaviors such as foraging and mate choice.
source: The majority of bird species rely on vision as their primary sensory modality, and color discrimination plays an important role in essential behaviors such as foraging and mate choice (Bennett and Théry, 2007).
evidence: This is established knowledge in avian biology, supported by a citation.

claim: Birds have evolved one of the most richly endowed color vision systems among vertebrates.
source: Accordingly, birds have evolved one of the most richly endowed color vision systems among vertebrates (Goldsmith, 1990).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: The avian color vision system relies on the coordinated spectral tuning of distinct cone photoreceptor subtypes (SWS1 and SWS2) via two very different mechanisms (opsin spectral tuning and carotenoid-based filtering).
source: Here, we have shown how this system relies on the coordinated spectral tuning of distinct cone photoreceptor subtypes (SWS1 and SWS2) via two very different mechanisms (opsin spectral tuning and carotenoid-based filtering).
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings of the study.

claim: These adaptations have served to enhance spectral sensitivity and color discrimination as birds have expanded their visual systems into the UV range.
source: Modeling suggests that these adaptations have served to enhance spectral sensitivity and color discrimination as birds have expanded their visual systems into the UV range.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the modeling results.

claim: Apocarotenoids are the major spectral filtering pigments within the C-type oil droplet of the SWS2 cone.
